title: SHE WAS PROMISED TO ANOTHER MAN. SHE WAS NOT FREE. THEN A MAN TOOK HER TO BED—AND GOD SAID SOMETHING THAT SHOULD MAKE US TREMBLE.
paragraphs: SHE WAS PROMISED TO ANOTHER MAN. SHE WAS NOT FREE. THEN A MAN TOOK HER TO BED—AND GOD SAID SOMETHING THAT SHOULD MAKE US TREMBLE.

Leviticus 19:20–22 | The disturbing law about a female servant, another man's betrothal, and a sacrifice for forgiveness—and what this difficult passage reveals about human vulnerability, unequal power, sexual sin, divine justice, and the mercy that ultimately leads us to Jesus Christ.
There are passages in the Bible that comfort you.
There are passages that strengthen you.
And then there are passages that make you stop reading, stare at the page, and whisper something you are almost afraid to say aloud.
“Lord… why is this in Your Word?”
This is one of those passages.
Because somewhere in ancient Israel, a woman was caught between two men.
She was promised to one.
She was sexually involved with another.
And she was not free.
Not free to determine her own future as an independent woman. Not free from the social realities of servitude. Not standing on equal ground with the men whose decisions could shape her life.
Then something happened that the law of Moses refused to leave unaddressed.
A sexual encounter.
A broken boundary.
A legal case involving a woman whose status made her especially vulnerable.
And a command from God that included accountability, sacrifice, and atonement.
But here is what makes this passage so unsettling.
The law does not describe the woman receiving the same punishment prescribed for certain other sexual offenses.
Instead, it introduces a distinction.
And unless we understand that distinction, we may misunderstand both the justice of God and the mercy of God.
Before you decide what this passage means, stay with me.

Because buried inside these ancient words is a question that reaches into our marriages, our churches, our private compromises, our treatment of vulnerable people, and the secrets we hope nobody discovers.
What happens when someone with greater power crosses a sexual boundary involving someone with less freedom—and what does God require when sin has already occurred?
The answer is more complicated than a slogan.
And more searching than many of us would prefer.
Listen carefully to the words of Leviticus 19:20–22 in the King James Version:

“And whosoever lieth carnally with a woman, that is a bondmaid, betrothed to an husband, and not at all redeemed, nor freedom given her; she shall be scourged; they shall not be put to death, because she was not free.
And he shall bring his trespass offering unto the LORD, unto the door of the tabernacle of the congregation, even a ram for a trespass offering.
And the priest shall make an atonement for him with the ram of the trespass offering before the LORD for his sin which he hath done: and the sin which he hath done shall be forgiven him.”
Read that again.
Slowly.
Because even the English translation raises difficult questions.
Why was the woman still enslaved?
What exactly did her betrothal mean?
Was the encounter consensual, coerced, or something the text does not tell us?
Why was the death penalty excluded?
Why did the man bring a guilt offering?
And perhaps the most uncomfortable question of all:
Does the Bible actually say that the woman was to be scourged?
That is where we must resist the temptation to rush toward an easy explanation.
If we love Scripture, we cannot defend it by pretending its difficult words are not there.
And if we love Jesus Christ, we cannot use the Bible to silence the very people whose suffering deserves careful attention.
The Hebrew text begins with a legal description:
וְאִישׁ כִּי־יִשְׁכַּב אֶת־אִשָּׁה
Ve'ish ki-yishkav et-ishah.
“And if a man lies with a woman…”
The expression describes sexual intercourse.
But then the law identifies the woman's condition.
וְהִוא שִׁפְחָה נֶחֱרֶפֶת לְאִישׁ
Vehi shifchah neḥerefet le'ish.
“And she is a female slave assigned or designated to a man…”
The Hebrew word shifchah refers to a female servant or slave.
The word neḥerefet is particularly difficult. It is rare, and its precise legal meaning is debated. Translators have rendered the phrase in terms of betrothal, assignment, or designation to a man.
That matters.
Because we must not simply imagine a modern engagement involving two independent people freely choosing a wedding date.
We are dealing with an ancient legal arrangement involving slavery, sexual obligations, and a woman's restricted status.
The text continues:
וְהָפְדֵּה לֹא נִפְדָּתָה אוֹ חֻפְשָׁה לֹא נִתַּן־לָהּ
Vehofdeh lo nifdatah, o ḥufshah lo nittan-lah.
“She has not been redeemed, nor has freedom been given to her.”
There it is.
The detail that changes how the entire case must be read.
She was not free.
The law repeats that reality when explaining why the ordinary capital penalty was not imposed.
כִּי־לֹא חֻפָּשָׁה
Ki lo ḥuppashah.
“Because she had not been freed.”
We must be precise here.

The text identifies her lack of legal freedom as the reason the death penalty does not apply in this case. It does not explicitly tell us whether she consented to the sexual encounter, whether coercion occurred, or what she personally experienced.
Those are questions we may rightly ask.
But we cannot answer them by inventing details that Moses did not record.
What we can say is that the law treats her status as legally significant.

In Deuteronomy 22:23–27, Israel's law distinguishes between different circumstances surrounding sexual intercourse involving a betrothed woman, including a case of forced intercourse in which the woman is explicitly declared innocent.
Leviticus 19:20–22 addresses a different situation.
It does not authorize us to flatten every sexual case into the same category.
Nor does it permit us to claim that all parties possessed equal freedom.
That would ignore the very condition the passage emphasizes.
And now we come to one of its most disputed expressions.
בִּקֹּרֶת תִּהְיֶה
Biqqoret tihyeh.
The King James Version renders this, “she shall be scourged.”
But the Hebrew term biqqoret is difficult, and its meaning in this context is uncertain.
Some interpretations understand it as punishment or disciplinary action. Others understand it as an inquiry, judicial investigation, or legally prescribed consequence.
This is why English translations differ.
The English Standard Version renders the phrase, “yet they shall not be put to death,” preceded by “a distinction shall be made.”
The New International Version speaks of “due punishment.”
The King James Version uses “she shall be scourged.”
These translations reflect real interpretive difficulties.
Therefore, we should not confidently insist that the Hebrew unambiguously commands a whipping of the woman, nor should we pretend that every interpretation removes the possibility of a penalty.
The exact legal procedure remains debated.
What is unmistakable is that the case is not treated as though nothing wrong happened.
The man must bring a ram as a guilt offering.
The priest must perform the prescribed rite of atonement.
The text identifies the man's conduct as sin.
And forgiveness is not described as something he simply declares over himself.
He must approach God according to the covenant's sacrificial requirements.
This is where the passage begins to confront us personally.
Because sin has a strange way of persuading us that if nobody knows, nobody has been harmed.
A private conversation.
A message deleted before someone else sees it.
A relationship hidden behind spiritual language.
A position of authority used to gain access to someone who feels unable to refuse.
A boundary crossed because one person had the power and the other person feared the consequences.
And sometimes the person with the greatest influence becomes the person most determined to control the story afterward.
But the God of Leviticus is not impressed by our ability to conceal things.
He sees what happens when the doors are closed.
He sees the intentions people disguise.
He sees the difference between genuine consent and compliance produced by fear.
He sees the person whose reputation is protected.
And He sees the person whose voice has been overlooked.
That does not mean Leviticus 19:20–22 answers every modern question about abuse, consent, or accountability.
It does not.
But the wider witness of Scripture leaves no room for treating exploitation as righteousness.
The Lord repeatedly commands justice for the vulnerable.
“The LORD executeth righteousness and judgment for all that are oppressed.” — Psalm 103:6, KJV
And later, through the prophet Isaiah, God commands His people to seek justice and defend those exposed to oppression (Isaiah 1:17).
The same Bible that records ancient slavery laws also confronts those who use power to harm others.
We must acknowledge the historical reality without pretending that regulating an institution is the same as endorsing every feature of that institution as God's eternal moral ideal.
The laws of ancient Israel were given within a particular covenant, society, and legal order.
They must be interpreted in their historical context and in light of the unfolding revelation of Scripture.
That is not an excuse to dismiss difficult verses.
It is a reason to study them carefully.
Because if we approach the Bible only looking for words that confirm what we already believe, we may miss the places where God is challenging us.
And perhaps that is where this story becomes painfully familiar.
Not because everyone reading has committed a sexual offense.
Not because every relationship involves exploitation.
But because nearly all of us understand the temptation to protect ourselves when truth threatens to expose something we would rather keep hidden.
We know what it means to minimize wrongdoing.
We know how easily people say, “It wasn't that serious.”
We know the temptation to ask whether something can be kept quiet instead of asking whether it was right.
And some reading this know another kind of pain.
The pain of being the person with less power.
The person who was pressured.
The person who feared losing a job, a relationship, a home, a ministry position, or the approval of someone influential.
The person who carried shame for something another person did.
If that is part of your story, hear this clearly.
Someone else's sin against you does not become your guilt simply because you were vulnerable.
And forgiveness never requires you to call evil good.
Christian grace does not demand that survivors abandon safety, silence their testimony, or restore trust before there is genuine repentance and accountability.
Jesus did not come to make darkness more comfortable.
He came as the Light.
And light does not heal by pretending wounds do not exist.
It reveals what must be addressed.
There is another danger here.
We could spend so much time studying the woman's legal status that we forget the passage explicitly requires the man to face his own wrongdoing.
Listen to the Hebrew expression used for his offering.
אָשָׁם
Asham.
A guilt offering, sometimes called a reparation offering.
The related language can carry ideas of guilt and liability.
In Leviticus, this offering belongs to a sacrificial system in which wrongdoing is not merely an unpleasant feeling to be forgotten.
Sin creates a real problem before a holy God.
And in this case, the man is not told to excuse himself by pointing to the woman's status.
He must bring the offering.
He must acknowledge that his action requires atonement.
He cannot turn his guilt into innocence simply by finding a technicality.
That should make every one of us examine the way we handle our own sins.
How many times have we been quicker to explain ourselves than to repent?
How many times have we blamed temptation instead of acknowledging our decisions?
How many times have we asked God to remove the consequences while resisting the transformation He calls us to pursue?
How many times have we wanted forgiveness without truth?
And how many times have we used religious words to avoid making things right with people we have harmed?
The offering in Leviticus was not a license to sin.
And the sacrifice of Jesus Christ is not a license to continue in sin either.
Paul asks in Romans 6:1–2 whether believers should continue in sin so that grace may abound.
His answer is unmistakable.
“God forbid.”
Grace is not permission to keep destroying what God calls holy.
Grace is the undeserved mercy that brings sinners into a new life.
But now the story becomes even more extraordinary.
Because the ram brought to the sanctuary in Leviticus was part of a sacrificial system that pointed beyond itself.
The blood of an animal was never the final answer to the human condition.
The letter to the Hebrews explains that the repeated sacrifices of the old covenant could not accomplish the ultimate removal of sin in the way Christ's sacrifice would.
Hebrews 10:4 declares:
“For it is not possible that the blood of bulls and of goats should take away sins.”
And Hebrews 10:10 tells us that believers are sanctified through the offering of the body of Jesus Christ once for all.
Do you see the movement?
From guilt to sacrifice.
From sacrifice to atonement.
From the repeated offerings of the old covenant to the once-for-all sacrifice of the Son of God.
This does not mean every detail of Leviticus 19:20–22 is a direct prediction about Jesus.
We must not force symbolism onto every feature of the law.
But the guilt offering belongs to the larger biblical sacrificial framework that finds its fulfillment in Christ.
And that changes how we understand forgiveness.
Because on the cross, Jesus did not announce that sin was harmless.
He bore its judgment.
He did not reveal a God who had stopped caring about holiness.
He revealed the astonishing depth of God's mercy toward sinners.
He did not die so that the powerful could escape accountability while the wounded were forgotten.
He died to reconcile sinners to God and create a redeemed people who walk in truth, justice, love, and holiness.
Isaiah 53:10 uses language connected with the Hebrew asham, often translated as a guilt offering.
Christians have long understood Isaiah's suffering servant passage in relation to Jesus' atoning death.
Here is the wonder of the Gospel.
The sinner cannot purchase divine forgiveness with excuses.
The sinner cannot erase guilt through religious performance.
The sinner cannot manufacture righteousness by controlling appearances.
But God has provided what sinners could never provide for themselves.
Jesus Christ.
The spotless Savior.
The crucified Redeemer.
The risen Lord.
And His grace reaches farther than our ability to repair ourselves.
But never confuse the reach of His grace with indifference toward the harm we cause.
The cross is where God's holiness and mercy meet—not where holiness disappears.
And that brings us to a moment in the Gospel of John.
A woman is brought before Jesus after being accused of adultery.
The crowd wants a judgment.
The religious leaders are testing Him.
And one detail should trouble anyone who reads the account carefully.
The woman is standing there.
But where is the man?
John 8 does not explain his absence.
We should not invent an answer.
Still, the scene confronts us with the danger of using a woman's shame as a weapon while the full circumstances remain unaddressed.
Jesus does not join the crowd's cruelty.
He exposes the accusers' own need to reckon with sin.
And when the accusers depart, He tells the woman:
“Neither do I condemn thee: go, and sin no more.” — John 8:11, KJV
Mercy.
And a call to change.
Compassion.
And holiness.

The account appears in John 7:53–8:11, a passage whose manuscript history is disputed because it is absent from many early Greek witnesses. That textual fact deserves acknowledgment. Yet the scene, as received in the Christian tradition, illustrates themes clearly taught elsewhere in Scripture: Jesus' mercy toward sinners and His call to repentance.
We should also recognize that this is not the same legal situation as Leviticus 19:20–22.
The women are not interchangeable.
Their circumstances are not identical.
But when these passages are read responsibly, they compel us to ask whether our treatment of sinners and vulnerable people reflects the character of the God we claim to worship.
Because it is possible to quote Scripture while refusing to practice mercy.
It is possible to speak passionately about holiness while hiding personal corruption.
It is possible to condemn another person's visible failure while protecting our own secret wrongdoing.
And it is possible to preach forgiveness without ever taking responsibility for what we have done.
That is not the transformation Jesus calls us into.
The Gospel demands more than a religious appearance.
It calls for a new heart.
A truthful confession.
A turning away from sin.
A willingness to repair harm where possible.
A life that begins to bear the fruit of repentance.
And for those who have suffered injustice, the Gospel also offers a Savior who understands suffering without suggesting that every wound will disappear overnight.
Jesus was betrayed.
Falsely accused.
Humiliated.
Stripped.
Abandoned.
Condemned.
He knows what it is to suffer at the hands of sinful people.
And His resurrection declares that cruelty, shame, and death will not have the final word.
Perhaps you are reading this as someone who has harmed another person.
You have rationalized it.
Hidden it.
Explained it away.
Perhaps you have convinced yourself that because time has passed, repentance is no longer necessary.
But time does not transform wrongdoing into righteousness.
Come into the light.
Confess your sin to God.
Stop the behavior.
Accept appropriate accountability.
Seek to make restitution where possible without pressuring the person you harmed to forgive you, contact you, or reconcile with you.
If abuse or a crime is involved, repentance does not replace lawful accountability or the need to protect others.
The mercy of Christ is real.
But genuine repentance refuses to make another person pay the price for our refusal to change.
And perhaps you are reading this as someone who has been harmed.
You have carried questions for years.
You have wondered why you were not protected.
You have heard people use religious language to make you feel responsible for what happened.
Please hear this.
You do not need to pretend you were unharmed in order to be faithful to Jesus.
You do not need to keep yourself in danger to prove that you have forgiven someone.
You can seek safety.
You can speak truth.
You can ask for help.
You can pursue justice.
You can grieve.
And you can bring your questions to God without having to manufacture an easy answer.
Psalm 34:18 says:
“The LORD is nigh unto them that are of a broken heart; and saveth such as be of a contrite spirit.”
God's nearness does not make every painful circumstance immediately understandable.
But your suffering is not invisible to Him.
And your worth does not depend on how another person treated you.
Now consider something else.
Leviticus 19 does not begin with this difficult sexual law.
It begins with a command that frames the entire chapter.
“Ye shall be holy: for I the LORD your God am holy.” — Leviticus 19:2, KJV
And within the same chapter comes one of the most important commands in all of Scripture:
“Thou shalt love thy neighbour as thyself: I am the LORD.” — Leviticus 19:18, KJV
Jesus later identifies love for God and love for neighbor as the two great commandments upon which the Law and the Prophets depend (Matthew 22:37–40).
Think about that.
The same chapter containing this disturbing legal case also commands holiness, honesty, justice, and love of neighbor.
That does not dissolve every historical difficulty.
But it prevents us from treating this passage as though its only purpose were to satisfy our curiosity about ancient sexual regulations.
Leviticus calls God's covenant people to be holy in the ordinary realities of life.
Not merely in worship ceremonies.
Not merely in what they say about God.
But in how they treat other people.
And Jesus brings that call into even sharper focus.
He does not merely command us to avoid certain outward acts.
He confronts the desires of the heart.
He condemns hypocrisy.
He calls His followers to servanthood rather than domination.
He warns against causing vulnerable people to stumble.
He teaches that greatness in His kingdom is not measured by the ability to control others.
It is revealed through humble service.
This is why the Christian response to Leviticus 19:20–22 cannot be to romanticize ancient slavery.
Nor can it be to claim that the text explicitly teaches every modern principle we wish it taught.
Faithfulness requires something more demanding.
We must recognize the law's historical setting, acknowledge its textual difficulties, understand its place in Israel's covenant, and read it in light of God's fuller revelation in Jesus Christ.
And we must allow its confrontation with sin to reach our own lives.
Because the deepest question is not simply whether we can explain a difficult passage.
It is whether we will submit to the God who speaks through Scripture.
Will we allow Him to expose our hypocrisy?
Will we surrender the sins we have learned to justify?
Will we stop confusing power with righteousness?
Will we defend people whose voices are easily ignored?
Will we receive grace without using it as an excuse to continue doing harm?
Will we believe that Christ can transform us without pretending transformation requires no repentance?
This is where the message becomes personal.
Maybe you are the person who has been hiding.
Maybe you are the person who has been wounded.
Maybe you are the believer who stopped reading Leviticus because the questions felt too disturbing.
Maybe you are the skeptic who wonders whether Christianity can honestly face its own difficult texts.
Or maybe you are the churchgoer who has spent years learning how to sound holy without ever allowing Jesus to touch the places where you are most afraid of being exposed.
Whoever you are, there is room here for an honest question.
And there is an invitation greater than pretending you have everything figured out.
Come to Christ.
Not because every historical question has been resolved.
Not because every wound has healed.
Not because every consequence has disappeared.
But because Jesus is the Savior sinners need, and He is worthy of our trust even when Scripture requires patient, difficult study.
First John 1:9 gives this promise:
“If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins, and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness.”
Notice what the promise does not say.
It does not say we must become skilled at hiding.
It does not say we must prove that someone else was worse.
It does not say we can purchase forgiveness.
It says confess.
Bring the truth before God.
And trust the faithfulness of the Savior.
That is why our message at Gospel Warrior is not that scandal is insignificant.
Scandal can devastate lives.
Sin can destroy trust.
Abuse can leave wounds that require years of care.
Consequences can remain even after genuine repentance.
But scandal does not have to be the final chapter of a sinner's life.
Jesus Christ can forgive.
Jesus Christ can redeem.
Jesus Christ can transform.
And Jesus Christ will ultimately judge with perfect righteousness.
From Scandal to Grace does not mean from wrongdoing to denial. It means from darkness to truth, from guilt to repentance, and from spiritual death to new life through Jesus Christ.
If this passage has unsettled you, do not rush to forget it.
Return to the verses.
Read Leviticus 19 in its entirety.
Compare careful Bible translations.
Ask the difficult questions.
And do not allow anyone to convince you that serious Bible study is a threat to genuine faith.
Truth does not need us to manufacture certainty where the Hebrew text leaves interpretive questions.
Truth calls us to humility.
And humility is not weakness.
It is one of the ways we acknowledge that God is God, and we are not.
I also want to ask something of you.
Not for an empty reaction.
Not for a comment written merely to increase numbers.
But for an honest response.

What struck you most deeply about this passage—the woman's lack of freedom, the man's responsibility, the difficulty of the Hebrew wording, or the way the guilt offering points us toward our need for Christ?
And if this article has brought you to a moment of personal repentance, you may simply write:
If you are struggling, you can write:
You do not need to disclose private trauma, identify someone who harmed you, or confess sensitive details publicly.
But you are welcome to share a testimony, a Scripture, a sincere question, or a prayer that might encourage another person.
Sometimes the most meaningful conversation begins when someone stops pretending to have all the answers.
And perhaps someone you know needs to read this.
Not because you want to embarrass them.
Not because you want to win an argument.
But because they are wrestling with the Bible, questioning God's character, carrying guilt, or struggling to understand how divine justice and divine mercy belong together.
Invite your family, your fellow believers, the person struggling with faith, and even the sincere skeptic who is willing to ask hard questions.
A thoughtful conversation about Scripture can open a door that an angry argument never could.

We are committed to exploring biblical truth, repentance, grace, forgiveness, restoration, and the transforming power of Jesus Christ—not merely the passages that are easy to share, but also those that require us to wrestle carefully with the Word.
There is something else I want to invite you into.
Gospel Warrior is more than a place to read an occasional article.
Our desire is to build a community of believers who do not merely consume spiritual content but grow deeper in their understanding of Scripture and their obedience to Christ.
These resources are intended to encourage biblical literacy, strengthen discipleship, and help people keep learning long after a social media post disappears from their feed.
It should not be confused with a mandatory biblical tithe, and it does not replace your responsibilities to your local church, family, or others in need.
You glorify Him through faith in Jesus Christ and a life of worship, obedience, love, truth, and generosity.
Second Corinthians 9:7 reminds us:
“God loveth a cheerful giver.”
Not a pressured giver.
Not a frightened giver.
Not someone made to believe that God's love or forgiveness depends on a payment.
A cheerful giver.
Someone whose generosity comes from a willing heart.
These products can be simple reminders of faith and opportunities to share biblical encouragement with others. They are not substitutes for prayer, Scripture, fellowship, or genuine discipleship.
You are still welcome here.
Read the free resources.
Study the Word.
Share what encourages you.
Pray for the ministry.
Help another person encounter the truth of Jesus Christ.
Your value in the body of Christ is not measured by a monthly payment.
The mission is to make Jesus known.
And that is why we keep returning to these difficult passages.
Because people do not need a faith that survives only when every verse is comfortable.
They need a faith rooted in the real Christ, who is worthy of our trust even when our understanding is incomplete.
They need Scripture handled with honesty.
They need grace that does not excuse sin.
They need holiness that does not become cruelty.
They need communities where vulnerable people are not silenced to protect reputations.
They need the courage to repent when they have done wrong.
They need the freedom to seek help when they have been harmed.
And above all, they need the Savior who died for sinners and rose again.
So return with me, one last time, to the ancient law.
A man.
A female servant.
A complicated betrothal.
A sexual offense.
A legal distinction.
A guilt offering.
An atonement.
A declaration of forgiveness.
And centuries later, a cross outside Jerusalem.
The two passages are not identical.
The cross does not erase the need to understand the law in its own historical context.
But the story of redemption moves us toward the One in whom forgiveness finds its ultimate foundation.
Jesus Christ.
The Lamb of God.
The Savior who does not need to distort justice in order to show mercy.
The Redeemer who calls sinners out of darkness rather than teaching them how to hide more effectively.
The Lord who is able to make people new.
And perhaps the most important question left by this passage is not whether you can explain every detail of ancient Israelite law.
Perhaps it is this:
When the truth finally reaches the place you have kept hidden, will you run farther into darkness—or will you bring it to Jesus?
Because the One who calls you to repentance is also the One who offers grace.
And the One who offers grace is the One who calls you into a transformed life.
The most beautiful thing about grace is not that Jesus helps us hide the truth about our past—it is that, through His mercy, our past no longer has to be the master of our future.
